title: Philippine Immigration Detention: If You Don't Pay, Your Deportation Never Moves
dek: A Chinese surfer was locked up in the Philippines for 41 days. What he saw wasn't a prison — it was a business with prices on everything: beds, boxed meals, phones, lawyers' fees. Every item had to be bought. Those who didn't pay were held for years, even over a decade.
why: StoryFM's Behind Bars series. Medium information density but solid detail. The first half is one man's ordeal; the second half — the gang economy inside the detention center, the ransom quotes from scam companies, the lawyers jacking up prices on the spot — is the part that's actually worth something.
who: Founders and going-global operators interested in the situation of overseas Chinese, the Philippine business environment, and the gray-industry and immigration-corruption machinery.
skip: 6:29-9:14 — the surfing career and startup background, unrelated to the core mechanism.

points.h: Immigration offered to release him on the spot for 1.5 million pesos
points.body: The night Feili was arrested, an immigration officer pulled him aside and said quietly, "I can help you." After the lawyer communicated, the word came back: give 1.5 million pesos, about 160,000-170,000 RMB, and you can walk out immediately, no problem at all. Of the 12 to 13 people picked up in the same sweep, nobody agreed to pay. Everyone thought it was impossible that such a thing could still exist in 2026, and wanted to resolve it through normal legal process. But the price of refusing was this: they were transferred from the holding cells of the General City police station to the Immigration Bureau's main detention center in Manila, where Feili ultimately spent 41 days.

points.h: When his phone was confiscated, the money in Gcash was transferred out
points.body: When Feili was detained his phone was taken, and they asked for his unlock code. He assumed it was normal procedure and gave it. His phone unlock code was the same as his Gcash payment password — the Philippine equivalent of Alipay. For the next four or five days he applied repeatedly and couldn't get the phone back, until he kept pressing the Chinese consulate and his lawyer, and it was finally returned. When he turned it on, the interface had all switched to English, and the Gcash transfer records showed money had been sent out — but then sent back the night before he got the phone. There was only about 1,000 RMB in it. Feili said it wasn't about the amount; it was that the phone had been touched while it wasn't in his hands. His read: many Chinese in Manila working in gray-industry scams who get arrested go through this same layer of skimming, but they don't dare go to the Chinese consulate, because their phones are full of criminal evidence.

points.h: The air conditioning and takeout the immigration officers described were real — in another form
points.body: For those unwilling to buy their own plane ticket to transfer, immigration would work on them in shifts, saying the Manila immigration facility was in great condition, had air conditioning, was very free — you could work out, play basketball, order takeout, use your phone. Feili said they weren't lying: there really was air conditioning, you really could order takeout — just in a completely different form. They arrived at the main detention center a little after 3 a.m. Getting out of the vehicle, what he saw was a square area, an outer layer of iron grating, a sheet-metal roof above, and on all sides iron cages like dog kennels, with communal sleeping platforms inside, hundreds of people. At 3 a.m. many weren't asleep — bare-chested, in nothing but underwear, hanging on the iron cages to stare at the newcomers. Feili said the few foreigners said nothing for several minutes after getting out, then it hit them: immigration had lied to them.

points.h: The detention center is a business invested in by a Chinese boss
points.body: What Feili heard inside was that this immigration detention center was invested in by a Chinese boss, in cooperation with the Immigration Bureau, and that the beds, toilets and other facilities were all newly built by that Chinese boss. Foreigners could just stay, but Chinese who came in had to pay. The lowest tier, a communal platform bed, was 10,000 pesos a month, about 1,100-1,200 RMB. Wealthy pan bosses and gambling kingpins could pay 50,000 pesos a month, about 6,000-plus RMB, for a so-called "air-conditioned room" — actually the same bed, just wrapped in tin foil and wooden boards, with a foam box of ice beside it, a hole cut in the box, and an exhaust fan pulling the cold air into the bed. That's where the Immigration Bureau's line about "there's air conditioning inside" came from.

points.h: Chinese gangs collect protection money: you want out without paying?
points.body: On Feili's first day inside, the head of the Chinese gang came to collect a "rumor fee," saying the facilities were all their investment and there was no way to stay for free. Feili said he had no money, he was here to serve time, how could he be expected to pay on top of that. The gang boss said, with a threatening tone: you're already in here and you don't want to spend money, and you still think you're getting out? Feili learned that the place is run by gangs, and the Chinese gang monopolizes everything for Chinese inmates — food, clothing, daily life — running a Chinese restaurant and a Chinese supermarket. The whole detention center held about 200 people; when Feili arrived it was the off season, and there were still over 100 Chinese, more than half of them gambling and gray industry. The Chinese gang's staff drew wages — the head chef 10,000 pesos a month, kitchen hands 5,000 pesos — very low pay, but many people couldn't get out precisely because they had no money for a lawyer, so they could only work to earn.

points.h: A Yunnan man held over a year; his family thought he'd died in Southeast Asia
points.body: A young man from Yunnan asked Feili for help. Before the pandemic he'd been lured to the Philippines by a high-salary recruitment ad; the moment he landed his phone and passport were taken and he was dragged into a compound to run telecom scams, and when his numbers were bad the supervisor shocked him with a stun baton every day. After the company was busted he served a few months, then was transferred to the immigration detention center. The normal deportation process is simple — a few departments sign off, you buy your own ticket, and you go — but immigration, in order to extract money, keeps you locked up a long time, and without paying the process doesn't move. He'd already been held over a year, with not a cent, no phone, eating only prison food every day, unable to reach his family, who thought he had died in Southeast Asia. Feili helped him write a letter in Chinese and translated it into English, and through an introduction from a Japanese man got to see the warden, who had a guard bring Feili's phone so the young man could add his father on WeChat and send a selfie and a voice message. Afterwards immigration bought a basic feature phone specifically to solve this problem.

points.h: Scam company ransom: 3 million pesos per person
points.body: The only Chinese Feili talked with much came from a scam company. The company's 70 or 80 people had been surrounded by immigration together with the police and the NBI, three agencies. The first wave of skimming was the NBI and police locking each person in a toilet — because there are no cameras in toilets — and taking everything valuable off them. The second wave was immigration negotiating with the company boss for the people: the quote differed per person, 1 million, 2 million, 3 million pesos, depending on the person in charge's mood. That company's deal was 3 million pesos per person, about 300,000-plus RMB. The boss ultimately ransomed 30 people — exactly the 30 held on one floor — and the rest were promised food deliveries until they got out. This young man ran an operation targeting the Japanese market, scamming middle-aged Japanese women; in his best month he made 2 million RMB and bought a house and a car in his small hometown county. Later he was kidnapped by a friend, had several hundred thousand transferred away, and was hit with a trumped-up illegal gun-possession charge by a corrupt cop, so he couldn't leave.

points.h: The Philippine lawyer raised his price on the spot when he saw he was Chinese
points.body: In Cebu, through an introduction from a Lithuanian, Feili met a Philippine lawyer who quoted 200,000 pesos, about 20,000-plus RMB, done in four weeks. After Feili got to Manila the lawyer came to visit, saw he was Chinese, and immediately raised the price, saying that was the old price and the new price required another 120,000 pesos, about 10,000-plus RMB. Feili decided not to use him and wrote off the deposit, turning instead to a Chinese middleman. The Chinese middleman quoted 30,000-plus RMB, four to six weeks, no more than six. Feili said the genuinely reliable Chinese middlemen know this procedural pipeline extremely well, because everyone locked up inside is Chinese. In the end he was held inside for over 30 days, 41 days total including Cebu. The Lithuanian who'd introduced the Philippine lawyer still hadn't gotten out when Feili messaged him.

But it's not about how much money it was. When the phone wasn't in my hands, it was transferred out.

Look at his corrupt bureaucratic system and his ordinary people as separate things. I still believe Filipinos are by nature very good people. But the bureaucratic system is truly too corrupt — and it drinks blood, the kind that drinks human blood.
